To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a non-Hermitic Hamiltonian with real spectrum can be treated as a quantum mechanical Hamiltonian with complex phase space; and (b) the resulting classical statistical mechanics can be obtained by integrating over this complex phase space.

the thermodynamics of PT-symmetric oscillating systems can be studied in a straightforward manner, and that the classical partition function of such systems can be obtained by integrating over complex phase-space variables.

(i) the quantum partition function is obtained by a straightforward WKB approximation; (ii) the classical partition function is obtained from the quantum one by a simple Wick rotation; (iii) the classical phase space is complex; (iv) the classical partition functions of the wrong-sign quartics are the same as those of the corresponding Hermitian ones, except for the integration contour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantum and classical statistical mechanics and thermodynamics of a class of PT-symmetric oscillatory potentials.
the thermodynamics of the quantum and classical statistical mechanics for a class of non Hermitian, PT symmetric, Hamiltonians.
the statistical mechanical properties of the quantum mechanical system described by the Hamiltonian $H = p^2 + x^2 - i \gamma x^4$.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for the class of PT-symmetric Hamiltonians considered, the quantum and classical partition functions, and the corresponding thermodynamic quantities, are identical.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thermodynamics of non-Hermetian PT-symmetric systems, in the classical limit, is not different from that of the corresponding Hermitian systems.
the non-Hermiticity of the Hamiltonian does not prevent the system from having a well-defined statistical mechanics.

non-Hermiticity can have significant consequences for thermodynamics, even when PT symmetry is preserved.
